Linking Pollen Deposition Dynamics to Plant-Pollinator Network Structure

Case study on Succisa pratensis (2022-2024)

Author

Jakub Štenc

The Conceptual Framework

Arceo-Gómez et al. (2016) argue that intraspecific variation in pollen receipt is not random. By plotting HP against CP for individual flowers, two distinct patterns typically emerge. These patterns act as a signature of the pollinator community structure.

Scenario A: The “Generalist” Assemblage (Type 1)

If the pollinator assemblage is even (many generalists contributing similarly), we expect Type 1 dynamics. These visitors carry mixed loads; therefore, as they deposit more CP, they inevitably deposit more HP.

  • Pattern: Linear positive relationship.

  • Ecological Driver: High pollinator evenness; generalized interactions.

Scenario B: The “Specialist/Uneven” Assemblage (Type 3)

If the assemblage is uneven (dominated by a few high-quality specialists and some “messy” low-quality generalists), we expect Type 3 dynamics. High-quality pollinators deposit pure CP (high CP, low HP), while incidental visitors deposit mostly HP (low CP, high HP).

  • Pattern: Exponential decrease (or “L” shape).

  • Ecological Driver: Low pollinator evenness; high variation in pollinator quality.

Abstract

Introduction

In plant-pollinator communities, plants often share pollinators with other species, leading to deposition of pollen from other species (Heterospecific Pollen) on the stigmas. This is a common phenomenon in nature with significant implications for plant reproduction and evolution and it has been studied in multiple systems (Arceo-Gómez et al., 2016). Based on previous studies, it is expected that the network structure (particularly pollinator evenness) may drive the pattern of conspecific and heterospecific pollen deposition on stigmas. However, the relationship between deposited pollen, pollinator evenness and pollinator pollen transfer capability is not well understood.

Pollen deposition dynamics

Pollen load and pollen feeding

The effect of the network properties to the pollen deposition dynamics

This study aims to determine if the composition of pollinator spectra of Succisa pratensis functionally constrains the plant to high heterospecific pollen (HP) receipt, and whether pollinator pollen body load and content of pollinator intestines explain the persistence of this pattern across years. We structure our analysis around three specific objectives:

  • Determine if the relationship between Conspecific (CP) and Heterospecific (HP) pollen deposition on Succisa stigmas follows a linear (generalist) or exponential (specialist-shielded) trajectory, and assess its stability across years.

  • Link the stigmatic deposition pattern to the “pollen transport quality” of the dominant visitors (e.g., Eristalis spp.). We hypothesize that the “Linear” pattern is driven by dominant visitors being “messy vectors,” carrying large conspecific loads but also significant heterospecific loads.

  • Assess whether the network evenness (the diversity of partners) correlates with the intensity of heterospecific pollen deposition. Following Arceo-Gómez et al. (2016), we test if high evenness drives Type 1 curves, even when absolute pollen pressure varies.

To do so, we employ data on pollen load and pollen feeding of pollinators, pollen deposition on stigmas, and network evenness, collected in 2022-2024 within a diverse plant-pollinator community with Succisa pratensis Moench (Caprifoliaceae) as the focal species.

ggplot(pollen_deposition, aes(x = conspecific_pollen, y = heterospecific_pollen, color = as.factor(year))) +

    geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, size = 1.2) + # Smoothed trend line

Code 
pollen_deposition <- pollen_deposition[!is.na(pollen_deposition$heterospecific_pollen), ] # Remove rows with NA in heterospecific_pollen

pollen_deposition$plant_id <- str_sub(pollen_deposition$id, end = -3) # Extract plant ID from stigma ID

model_linear_mixed <- lme(
    heterospecific_pollen ~ conspecific_pollen * year, # Fixed effect: conspecific pollen and year
    random = ~ 1 | plant_id, # This tells R: "Group stigmas by inflorescence"
    data = pollen_deposition
)

summary(model_linear_mixed)
Code 
test_curve_shape <- function(year_data, year_label) {
    # 1. Fit Linear Model (Type 1)
    fit_linear <- lm(heterospecific_pollen ~ conspecific_pollen, data = year_data)

    # 2. Fit Exponential Model (Type 3)
    fit_exp <- tryCatch(
        {
            nls(heterospecific_pollen ~ a * exp(b * conspecific_pollen),
                data = year_data,
                start = list(a = max(year_data$heterospecific_pollen), b = -0.01)
            )
        },
        error = function(e) NULL
    )

    # 3. Compare AIC
    aic_lin <- AIC(fit_linear)
    aic_exp <- if (!is.null(fit_exp)) AIC(fit_exp) else NA

    return(data.frame(
        Year = year_label,
        Linear_AIC = round(aic_lin, 2),
        Exp_AIC = round(aic_exp, 2),
        Best_Fit = ifelse(!is.na(aic_exp) && aic_exp < (aic_lin - 2), "Exponential (Type 3)", "Linear (Type 1)")
    ))
}

# Run the test
results_2022 <- test_curve_shape(subset(pollen_deposition, year == 2022), "2022")
results_2023 <- test_curve_shape(subset(pollen_deposition, year == 2023), "2023")
results_2024 <- test_curve_shape(subset(pollen_deposition, year == 2024), "2024")

# Display Results
knitr::kable(rbind(results_2022, results_2023, results_2024), caption = "Model Comparison Results")

# 2. Calculate Similarity (Beta Diversity)
# Pivot to wide format as required by calculate_similarity
wide_interaction_data <- interaction_data_Succisa_22_24 %>%
    dplyr::select(year, plot_id, pollinator_id, rate) %>%
    # Aggregate rates by summing interactions across all samples within the plot (handle NAs)
    tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = pollinator_id, values_from = rate, values_fill = 0, values_fn = function(x) sum(x, na.rm = TRUE)) # Ensure no NAs in aggregation

# Calculate full similarity matrix
sim_results <- calculate_similarity(wide_interaction_data, group_by = c("year", "plot_id"))

# Visualize using package function
p_similarity <- plot_similarity_change(sim_results, plot_type = "within_year_heterogeneity") +
    labs(
        title = "B. Community Similarity",
        subtitle = "Pairwise within year (Ruzicka)"
    ) +
    theme(legend.position = "none")

# 3. Combine Plots
# Ensure ggpubr or patchwork is available. Using ggpubr as it is a dependency of HanPolNet.

ggpubr::ggarrange(p_evenness, p_similarity, ncol = 2)

Proposed Analysis

We test our hypothesis using independent datasets for both the curve (pollen counts) and the driver (visitation networks), following our three-step logic:

Step 1: The Pattern (Validation)

For each year of Succisa data (2022-2024), we fit two models to the stigmatic pollen counts to characterize the CP-HP relationship: 1. Linear Model (Type 1): \(HP \sim CP\) 2. Exponential Model (Type 3): \(HP \sim a \cdot e^{b \cdot CP}\)

We assess whether the “linear” pattern (ecological exposure to HP) persists across years despite variations in pollinator abundance.

Step 2: The Mechanism (Body Loads)

We analyze the “pollen transport quality” of dominant visitors by examining their body loads (and potentially gut contents). We test if the dominant visitors (e.g., Syrphids) carry mixed loads (high CP and high HP), effectively acting as “messy vectors” that drive the Type 1 relationship.

Step 3: The Driver (Network Evenness)

We calculate Simpson’s Evenness for the sub-network of visitors to Succisa pratensis for each year. We then link this network metric to the deposition pattern: - Hypothesis: Years/Sites with Type 1 (Linear) curves correspond to higher pollinator evenness. - This tests if the network structure (high variation in partners) functionally prevents the plant from escaping heterospecific pollen.

Why This Matters

This moves our analysis beyond simple abundance (“we found less HP”) to functional mechanisms.

If we confirm that Succisa fits a Type 3 curve in years with low evenness, it suggests that “pollinator sharing” (a network metric) does not translate linearly to pollen deposition. It would prove that the identity and quality of specific visitors shield the plant from heterospecific pollen interference, even when surrounded by heterospecific neighbors.
